submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on the token that supplies the clause's indefinite 'how much / how often' operator rather than its lexical content: approximative and frequency adverbs (rather, quite, very, really, largely, partly, generally, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, previously, probably), indefinite quantifier, possessive and demonstrative determiners (some, both, all, any, much, other, own, its, their, this), extent adjectives used attributively (considerable, significant, enormous, mounting), and the durative extent predicates they attach to (remained, remains, persists, extended). It is retrospective and stays at baseline on the definite article 'the', on content nouns and prenominal nouns (the plan, the budget, the evidence, the agency costs), and on exact/extreme degree adverbs (extremely, totally, completely, fairly, slightly, roughly, always, never); in the scan's Norwegian/Danish documents the same grammatical-not-lexical content sits in the word's final suffix token (-lig, -else, -et), where the pole also peaks.

rival_explanations: A broad closed-class reading: the pole fires on high-frequency grammatical words in general (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries, pronouns), and the adverb and quantifier peaks are simply the most common members of that class, so 'the', 'of' and 'is' should fire as strongly as 'some' and 'rather'.

A narrow adverbial reading: only the handful of high-frequency approximative and frequency adverbs (rather, quite, very, often, generally, usually) really drive the pole, and the determiner and attributive-adjective peaks are spillover from adjacent tokens, so 'some', 'both' and 'considerable' should not fire in isolation.

A morphological reading: the pole is really a detector of long words' final subword tokens (the Norwegian -lig/-else/-et peaks and the 'ational', 'able', 'ens' peaks in the top examples), and the English modifier peaks are just short function words that the tokenizer leaves whole.

pH triggered reversible photoinduced electron transfer to and from carbon nanoparticles.
Dopamine functionalized carbon nanoparticles (CNPs) that can act as efficient photoinduced electron donor-acceptor systems depending on the pH of the medium have been synthesized. In acidic media, dopamine on CNPs exists as hydroquinone and serves as an electron donor while under alkaline conditions the corresponding quinone form of dopamine serves as a strong electron acceptor. Application of external NADH to the system can invert the donor-acceptor roles under alkaline conditions.

Let There Be Love (Christina Aguilera song)

"Let There Be Love" is a song recorded by American singer-songwriter Christina Aguilera for her seventh studio album, Lotus (2012). It was written and produced by Max Martin and Shellback, with additional writing from Bonnie McKee, Oliver Goldstein, Oscar Holter and Jakke Erixson. Having originally collaborated with other producers in her earlier works, Aguilera stated that the "full circle" her career had taken became the right time to work with Martin. The song combines dance-pop, EDM and pop music genres, and is influenced by electronica and trance. Its instrumentation incorporates synths, drums and electronics.

"Let There Be Love" garnered positive reviews from music critics. Many praised Aguilera for not over singing and delivering a solid vocal performance, while others complimented the musical structure and composition. The song peaked at number 132 on the South Korea international singles chart following the release of the album, and at number one on the US Hot Dance Club Songs chart.

On August 29, 2013, an accompanying music video for the song was released on Aguilera's official channel. It features cameo appearances from Nicole Richie, Christina Milian, Chris Mann, Aguilera's son Max Bratman and her current boyfriend Matthew Rutler. The video sees everybody makes the "L" sign for the word "love", alongside positive messages, such as "Racism sucks", "Accept", and "Amo a mi hijo gay" ("I love my gay son"). It was described as a "soulful, and completely inexplicable, letter to her fans thanking them for their undying love". To promote Lotus and the song, Aguilera performed "Let There Be Love" at the 40th American Music Awards and on The Voice in the United States.

Background and recording

Following the release of her sixth studio album, Bionic (2010), Aguilera filed for divorce from her husband Jordan Bratman, starred in her first feature film, Burlesque and recorded the accompanying soundtrack. She then became a coach on NBC's singing competition show The Voice and appeared as a featured artist on Maroon 5's single "Moves Like Jagger" (2011), which spent four weeks atop the US Billboard Hot 100 chart. Following these events, Aguilera announced that had plans to begin production of her seventh album, stating that she wanted high quality and "personal" songs for the record. Regarding the creative direction, she revealed that the album would be a "culmination of everything I've experienced up until this point... I've been through a lot since the release of my last album, being on (' The Voice '), having had a divorce... This is all sort of a free rebirth for me." She further said "I'm embracing many different things, but it's all feel-good, super-expressive [and] super-vulnerable." Aguilera continued to say that the album would be about "self – expression and freedom" because of the personal struggles she had overcome during the last couple of years.

# 5. Wave Optics

Why is visible light not optimal for microscopes or computer chips? Short Answer: Visible Light has wave properties and the interactions of these waves are not always ideal. We can no longer use the ray model of light - we must use the wave model.

Diffraction: the behavior of a wave when it encounters an obstacle in its medium. Diffraction, in general causes a wave to bend around obstacles and make patterns of strong and weak waves. Diffraction can be useful (such as using x-rays to find bones) or unhelpful (such as light entering telescopes)

Incoherent light: When multiple parts of the light wave are out of step from with each other and have different phase constants (ex. light from the sun)

Coherent light: When all parts of the wave are in step and have the same phase constant (light from a laser beam)

Diffraction angles depend only on the unit-less ratio of  λ/d in which λ = wavelength and d = center to center spacing between the slits.

### Correspondence Principle:

When λ/d is small (< 10-4), the ray model of light and the wave model of light must give approximately the same result.

### Huygen's Principle

Huygen's principle is used to describe the constructing and destructing interference that occurs between waves in a double slit experiment

It states that "any wavefront can be broken down into many small side-by-side wave peaks, which then spread out as circular ripples, and by the principle of superposition, the result of adding up these sets of ripples must give the same result as allowing the wave to propagate forward.

adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests the definite article and content/prenominal nouns with no indefinite quantifier or degree operator, which the hypothesis puts at baseline.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The committee was extremely careful about the schedule, and the evidence was totally clear to everyone at the agency.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests the named exact/extreme degree adverbs 'extremely' and 'totally', which the hypothesis explicitly places at baseline.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The agency costs rose slightly and the budget was roughly unchanged from the previous quarter, according to the report.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests the exact degree adverbs 'slightly' and 'roughly', named as baseline in the hypothesis, in a topical budget sentence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The report was fairly accurate on the main points, but the analysis was completely wrong about the cause of the failure.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests 'fairly' and 'completely', which the hypothesis names as exact/extreme degree adverbs that stay at baseline.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The staff always arrive early and the doors never close before the evening shift ends at the depot.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests the frequency adverbs 'always' and 'never', which the hypothesis lists among the baseline extreme adverbs.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: They would rather sell the building than accept the offer, so the agency withdrew from the negotiation over the lease.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests 'rather' in its preference-modal sense, which supplies no how-much/how-often operator, so the hypothesis predicts baseline.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The agency review of the budget documents found the evidence clear on the central question about the funding.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests bare prenominal nouns and content nouns in a nominal chain with the definite article and no operator.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: They travelled by train rather than by bus because the roads were closed after the storm last week.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests 'rather' inside the comparative 'rather than' construction, where it marks an alternative rather than an approximative degree.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The navigational charts were reviewed by the committee before the voyage, and the appendix listed the changes.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests a long relational adjective in attributive position ('navigational', tokenized ' navig'|'ational'): the hypothesis predicts baseline for a non-extent modifier, while the morphological reading predicts a peak on the final 'ational' token.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The mounting of the photograph on the board took two hours before the frame arrived at the office.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Same-word, other-sense negative: 'mounting' is the noun for the act of fixing a photograph, not an attributive extent adjective, so the hypothesis predicts baseline.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The program stores each network address in the table and the server reads it at boot every morning.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Same-word, other-sense negative: 'address' is the computer-science noun, a content noun the hypothesis predicts stays at baseline.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She addresses the audience every morning before the session begins, and the staff takes notes during the talk.

readings.explanation: The pole fires on the token that supplies the clause's indefinite 'how much / how often' operator rather than its lexical content: approximative and frequency adverbs (rather, quite, very, really, largely, partly, generally, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, previously, probably), indefinite quantifier, possessive and demonstrative determiners (some, both, all, any, much, other, own, its, their, this), extent adjectives used attributively (considerable, significant, enormous, mounting), and the durative extent predicates they attach to (remained, remains, persists, extended). It is retrospective and stays at baseline on the definite article 'the', on content nouns and prenominal nouns (the plan, the budget, the evidence, the agency costs), and on exact/extreme degree adverbs (extremely, totally, completely, fairly, slightly, roughly, always, never); in the scan's Norwegian/Danish documents the same grammatical-not-lexical content sits in the word's final suffix token (-lig, -else, -et), where the pole also peaks.

A broad closed-class reading: the pole fires on high-frequency grammatical words in general (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries, pronouns), and the adverb and quantifier peaks are simply the most common members of that class, so 'the', 'of' and 'is' should fire as strongly as 'some' and 'rather'.

A narrow adverbial reading: only the handful of high-frequency approximative and frequency adverbs (rather, quite, very, often, generally, usually) really drive the pole, and the determiner and attributive-adjective peaks are spillover from adjacent tokens, so 'some', 'both' and 'considerable' should not fire in isolation.

A morphological reading: the pole is really a detector of long words' final subword tokens (the Norwegian -lig/-else/-et peaks and the 'ational', 'able', 'ens' peaks in the top examples), and the English modifier peaks are just short function words that the tokenizer leaves whole.
